issues.legal_issue: In a landlord’s ejectment appeal, equal comparative hardship does not support an ejectment order in the landlord’s favour unless an additional circumstance warrants preferring the landlord.
material_facts: The appellate court found that hardship to the landlord and tenant would be the same.
The appellate court’s finding was confirmed by the High Court.
issues.conclusion: If comparative hardship is equal, an ejectment order in the landlord’s favour cannot be made in the absence of an additional circumstance indicating that the landlord should be preferred.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the principle that equal comparative hardship, without an additional circumstance justifying preference for the landlord, does not permit an ejectment order in the landlord’s favour. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: landlord_ejectment_appeal and comparative_hardship_equal and not preference_supporting_circumstance

predicates.landlord_ejectment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in an ejectment suit brought by a landlord.
predicates.comparative_hardship_equal: The court found that the hardship to the landlord and tenant would be the same.
predicates.preference_supporting_circumstance: An additional circumstance was found that indicated the landlord should be preferred.
predicates.landlord_favoring_ejectment_order_unavai: An ejectment order in the landlord’s favour cannot be made.

issues.definition: When a landlord’s ejectment appeal involves equal comparative hardship and no circumstance indicating preference for the landlord, an ejectment order in the landlord’s favour is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate determination of comparative hardship must consider the applicable hardship rule, and failure to do so may require the prior order to be set aside and the matter remanded for reconsideration.
material_facts: The appellate court did not consider Rule 16(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972 when addressing comparative hardship.
The High Court confirmed the appellate court’s order.
The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and remanded the appeal for reconsideration of comparative hardship under Rule 16(2).
issues.conclusion: The order was set aside and the matter remanded for the appellate court to reconsider comparative hardship in light of Rule 16(2). The appellate court could consider the earlier agreement, the tenant’s offer to return his own shop to the landlord, and the equities of the case, and the parties could submit additional evidence by affidavit.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 16(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972 had to be considered in assessing comparative hardship. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.landlord_ejectment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in an ejectment suit brought by a landlord.
predicates.applicable_hardship_rule_not_considered: The appellate court did not consider the applicable rule when assessing comparative hardship.
predicates.prior_order_set_aside_and_matter_remande: The prior order is set aside and the matter is remanded for reconsideration of comparative hardship.

issues.definition: When an appellate court in a landlord’s ejectment appeal does not consider the applicable hardship rule, the prior order is set aside and the matter is remanded for reconsideration of comparative hardship.
